title: A Live Stats Panel for Your Game
summary: With Delve publishing its telemetry, a separate tool can show it live: frame times with a graph, the floor, the player's health and position, how many monsters are alive. This lesson builds that tool as a console program (chapter 14 gives it a graphical interface): finding running copies of the game, reading snapshots on a timer, keeping a history for graphs, and coping when the game starts, stops or restarts.
markdown:
## What the panel shows

```
 Delve telemetry · pid 18324 · v1                      connected
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 frame 48211       frame time 7.9 ms   (min 6.8 · avg 8.2 · max 21.4)
 ▁▁▂▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▇▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▂▁▁▁▁   last 60 samples
 floor 3     turn 412     player (17, 9)     hp 14 / 20 ███████░░░
 monsters alive 6
```

Every value comes from one consistent snapshot (lesson 12.04). The graph shows the last 60 frame times, scaled so the slowest is the tallest bar, and the spike in it is exactly the kind of stutter lesson 8.08 warned about, now visible while playing.

## Finding the game

The telemetry block's name includes the game's process id (lesson 12.04), so the tool:

1. Lists processes named `delve.exe` (lesson 6.07's snapshot).
2. For each, tries `OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_READ, FALSE, L"Local\\Delve.Telemetry.<pid>")`.
3. Maps the first that opens and checks `magic`, `version` and `size` before reading anything else (lesson 12.06 covers what to do with versions it does not know).

If several copies are running, it can show a list to choose from.

## The read loop

```cpp-norun
while (running)
{
    TelemetryV1 snap{};
    if (!connected) tryConnect();
    else if (!readSnapshot(block, snap)) showStatus("busy");          // retries exhausted (lesson 12.04)
    else if (snap.frame == lastFrame) staleFor += interval;           // the game is paused, or frozen
    else { staleFor = 0; lastFrame = snap.frame; history.push(snap.frameMs); draw(snap, history); }

    if (connected && !processStillRunning(pid)) disconnect();         // the game exited: start looking again
    Sleep(100);                                                       // 10 updates a second is plenty for people
}
```

Three states matter and should be shown clearly:

| State | Detect | Show |
|---|---|---|
| **Connected and live** | The frame number advances | The values |
| **Connected but stale** | The frame number has not changed for a second | "paused or not responding", values greyed out |
| **Not connected** | No mapping found, or the process exited | "waiting for Delve...", and keep looking |

Checking whether the process is still running uses a process handle opened with `SYNCHRONIZE` and `WaitForSingleObject(handle, 0)` (lesson 6.01: a process handle is signalled when it exits). The mapping itself stays valid while the tool has it open, even after the game exits, so the frame counter alone cannot tell "exited" from "frozen".

## Drawing in the console

Lesson 5.09's techniques do the drawing: enable virtual terminal sequences, build the whole screen into one string starting with "cursor home", and write it in one call so it never flickers. The bars use the Unicode block characters `▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█`, written in UTF-8 after `SetConsoleOutputCP(CP_UTF8)`. The practice task computes the statistics and the bar characters from the history.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Treating an unchanged frame number as "the game exited"
> It also means paused or frozen. Check the process handle separately.

> [!warning] Reading as fast as possible
> People cannot read 1,000 updates a second, and it wastes a core. 10 to 30 per second is plenty.

> [!warning] Crashing when the game restarts
> Unmap, close and go back to searching; the new copy has a new process id and a new block.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What three connection states should a monitoring tool show?
+ Live, stale (paused or frozen), and not connected
- Starting, running and closed
- Fast, slow and very slow
- Debug, Release and unknown
> Stale and not connected look similar in the numbers but mean very different things to the person watching.

? How does the tool find the game's telemetry?
- It searches the whole of memory for the magic number
- It reads a file the game writes to the desktop
+ It opens the mapping named with each `delve.exe`'s process id
- It attaches as a debugger and reads the game's variables
> Naming the mapping with the process id keeps two running copies of the game apart. It opens it read-only and checks the header before trusting it.

? How does the panel draw without flickering?
- It clears the console before each line
- It redraws only once per second
- It uses a second console window
+ It writes the whole screen as one string, once
> Clearing and redrawing line by line is what causes flicker.

? How does the tool tell "the game is paused" from "the game has exited"?
+ By whether its process handle is signalled
- Both are shown by the frame number
- The tool cannot tell
> The mapping outlives the game while the tool holds it open.

? Why does the tool include the process id when opening the mapping?
- Mapping names must be numbers
+ Each running copy uses a name with its id
- To make the name secret
> It lets several copies run side by side.

? How often should a stats panel read snapshots?
- As fast as possible
- Once a minute
+ About 10 to 30 times a second
> Faster than people can read wastes CPU for nothing.
```
ideas:
- Build the console panel and run it next to Delve. Make the game stutter (allocate a big block in one frame) and spot it in the graph.
- Start the panel before the game, then close and restart the game, and check the panel follows.
- Add a second graph for monsters alive over the last minute.
